utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. I assume my learned friends will call a new witness. However, before this I ask leave to be allowed to speak about protective measures. So I ask that we go into private session. I wish to put forward the joint position of all the Defence teams as regards the protective measures granted to witnesses, and in particular the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is well-known that proceedings in this Tribunal, essentially public, and for that reason in most cases witnesses give their evidence in the ordinary way and their identity and that therefore of their family is well-known to the public and all. It is equally well-known that in trials in this Tribunal there are a variety of circumstances in witness -- in which witnesses are or for sound reasons feel that they are threatened in their personal security or in the personal security of their families. For that reason, the Rules provide that applications may be made for protective measures, the purpose of that scheme is to ensure the personal safety of witnesses and their families. To justify protective measures, the party applying, whether it be Defence or Prosecution, for protective measures must satisfy the Chamber that there are sound reasons that go to the personal security of the witness or the witness's family to justify those protective measures. Because of the nature of a number of those reasons, the Rules allow for applications to be made by either party ex parte, and there are cases where Defence witnesses require protective measures for reasons which are not disclosed to the Prosecution, just as there are cases where Prosecution witnesses require protective measures on the same basis. In this case, application was made. The Defence responded, although as has been indicated by Mr. Lukic basically without detailed knowledge. But the Defence did not object to the protective measures that were sought in respect of this and the other witnesses that have been mentioned, that is, P-21, 29, 31, 32. The material offered ex parte by the Prosecution satisfied the Chamber that there were reasons which justified the protective measures that have been ordered. They were reasons dealing with the present and future personal security of the witness and/or the witness's family. The Chamber saw nothing which went to the merits of the case or, in particular, to the credibility of the witness. The Chamber is conscious that those are issues which are important that the Defence be aware of in the case of a Prosecution application. For that reason, the Chamber was persuaded to grant the measures and to do so on the ex parte application. We are not, of course, for those reasons minded to make any variation to the orders that have been made. We would add that in the particular case of the next witness, Mr. Agha has been helpful enough to indicate very briefly the essence of the reason which justified in the case of this witness a change from the position obtained when the witness gave evidence some seven years ago, and that is personal harassment and harassment of the children of the witness. We would ask the Prosecution as a matter of helpfulness and courtesy if they could look at the reasons relating to these reasons -- to these potential witnesses, and if they feel that they can make those available to the Defence on the confidential basis that they are part of an ex parte motion, we would encourage that just as a means of enabling the Defence to see that these were matters that went to personal security and were not dealing with the merits of the case. Now, we encourage that; we do not make an order to that effect. We encourage it because of the cooperative spirit shown by Mr. Agha and because there will be some cases where information can be made available on a confidential basis without producing any significant problem for the witness. That having been said, we would not make any change to the formal orders that have been made. Mr. Agha, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honours. This witness, as we know, has protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will go into open session. If the witness could be called. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate for the record that there is no reason why the decision of the Chamber on that application should be in private session. It may be included in the open transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you read out the solemn declaration on the card that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May we go into private session while we deal with the pseudonym, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in early 1991 you were working as a doctor in Vukovar Hospital. What was the situation like in Vukovar in early 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a completely normal situation, normal living circumstances, typical for a small town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the conditions like at the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Completely normal working conditions for a hospital of that size and hospital that satisfied all the needs of the residents of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it a mixed area ethnicity-wise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in spring of 1991, was there an event which changed the atmosphere in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early May 1991, an incident took place, following which many other changes occurred in Vukovar, at least I can trace those changes back to that incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that incident, in brief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an incident which took place in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May. If I can describe it properly, it was a police intervention in Borovo Selo which resulted in the killing of about 11 policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these policemen of a particular ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say that with certainty. I couldn't say that all of them belonged to the same ethnicity. I don't think I would be accurate in saying that. Most of them were Croats. Now, as to whether there were other ethnicities in that group, I couldn't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did this incident affect the atmosphere in Vukovar after May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People started feeling insecure. I think that the relations between people also changed. There was a lack of trust among people. It is generally difficult to describe that situation in just a few words, but people were scared. They didn't know what to expect. They didn't know what would ensue, and they didn't know what attitude to take in relation to the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did these tensions continue to grow as 1991 wore on between the different communities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. As I said, relations between people changed. They ceased being so friendly and open. One could feel the tension in daily contacts in stories exchanged by friends. The situation was, I would say, very strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the incident you mention in May 1991 where the police officers were killed, did this -- after this time, did this have an affect on the staffing levels at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. In the course of May and June there was a decrease in the number of staff members. Many people stopped coming to work on both sides. And the number of personnel decreased significantly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "both sides," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I speak of people, it's hard for me because I do not distinguish among them only on the basis of their ethnicity. I just see them as people. Unfortunately, in this case I have to say "both sides." And when I say "both sides," I mean both Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, despite elements of both sides leaving the hospital, creating the staffing shortages, but did also elements of both sides remain at the hospital and continue to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. I think that was the personal choice of every individual. I don't think that anybody was forced to make the decision. I think that it was a personal choice in each case, whether to leave or to stay. That is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time in 1991 when the city of Vukovar itself came under attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first attack that I remember, attack of a larger scale, although even prior to that there were instances of shelling, but the real attack on this city took place on the 25th of August, 1991, when the town was shelled for the first time, the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of weaponry was used to shell Vukovar? Was it heavy or light arms fire or aircraft? What kind of weaponry was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that perhaps I won't be fully accurate in this case because, after all, I'm a physician and I'm not very familiar with weapons. But what I can claim with certainty is that on the 25th of August bombing took place. I personally saw airplanes because I was outside and I was personally at risk from those planes. In addition to that, I can say with certainty that shells were fired because shells landed in the vicinity of my house as well. Now, as to the type of shells, it's hard for me to say. I think that that falls in the category of heavy weaponry, and I apologise in advance if I made any mistakes because I'm not competent in this area. You know, when they fire at you, then things are difficult for you. You find everything hard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was shelling Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they were shelling Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it wasn't clear to me. Why would anybody want to shell Vukovar? There was no need to do that. We led a normal life. It was just a regular life of a small, unremarkable city. I personally saw no need in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mention that the shelling was heavy artillery or shells. How extensive was it? Was it once a week or once a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially in June and July, it would take place perhaps once a day or once every two days. It's hard to be quite specific. But as the time went by, as the days streamed by, the intensity grew on a daily basis. So that towards the end, that is to say in November, we had a feeling that not a single minute went by without shelling and firing. In order to depict this clearly to you, I will say to you that the quiet constituted a greater problem for us because it started bothering us, we were so unused to it. And once the shelling would commence, then the situation would go back to normal for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned it was the shelling of Vukovar. Now, obviously Vukovar is a city. In particular, where you worked, the hospital, was that also shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that with certainty because I, myself, was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it also shelled quite extensively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the last month or two, on a daily basis. I don't know whether a minute went by when it was not shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you were working at a hospital. So were there any kind of markings to indicate that this building was in fact a hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there had to be markings. We had a clear and visible marking with a red cross on it. It was placed in the meadow in a plateau, or rather, on the lawn between the buildings. And it was clearly visible from the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yet these markings didn't stop the bombings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the hospital was extensively shelled. How much damage was actually done to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the moment the attacks started, the building would be damaged on a daily basis. Initially, the damage was only on the upper storeys of the hospital. And occasionally, certain parts of each of the upper floors would cave in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from August when you mentioned the attack starts, I think August the 25th you mentioned, what were the working conditions like in the hospital for a doctor and patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In August, the conditions were already somewhat difficult in view of the situation that existed in town. But we could still carry on with our daily activities in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did these conditions improve or not improve as time progressed into September and October and November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The conditions deteriorated daily and it became more and more difficult to ensure normal working conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much running water did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had running water on a daily basis sometime until September [as interpreted], when the normal water supply to the hospital was terminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you manage for water after the supply was terminated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially, we had cisterns, water tanks, that would arrive in the hospital. Later on it became impossible to transport water in this way because people were injured and died doing that. We had a case when one person who had transported water to the hospital was killed in the hospital compound. Unfortunately, we had to transport water in various containers from the Danube and from nearby wells and we had to do it during the night to bring the water to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you kindly. I have a correction for the transcript. Page 14, line 11. I think that the witness stated that they had running water until September or October, and the transcript reflects only September. The witness said "September or October 1991."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you clarify that, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, learned Defence counsel has indicated that when I asked you a question as to how long you had running water, you replied that it was September or October. But the transcript only reveals September. So can you please clarify when running water to the hospital ceased.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's hard to be specific about the date. I apologise, but I will always point out when I am not quite sure about the time reference. I hope you will understand this. When you spend three months shut in one area, whether something happened ten days before the date or 15 days after it, it really wouldn't mean much to us under those circumstances. I know the date is very important for you, and thus I have to apologise for not being available to be quite specific. It was either in late September or early October. I hope you will have understanding for this. It's not that I want to exaggerate or diminish something, but please be understanding about me not being able to be quite specific about time period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you say that the supply of water was terminated. Do you know how it came to be terminated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was discontinued because the water supply structure, the pipes that brought the water to the hospital, were damaged. The pipeline was damaged by shelling, and as a result of that there was no water supply in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that the water supply was terminated. What about electricity? Did you have functioning electricity supply throughout the period you were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Likewise, until a certain period of time we had regular electricity supply in all parts of the hospital. But once again, in view of all the factors I listed just prior to this, due to damage to the electrical supply equipment, we did not have continuous supply of electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how was, actually, the hospital able to operate, carry out operations, et cetera, without sufficient electricity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those cases, all hospitals have special generators in order to supply the indispensable rooms so that they could function. In this case, we used generators to supply operating rooms with electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were medicines able to freely come in and out of the hospital during this period, between August and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The moment normal communication with Vukovar was terminated, we had only the medication that was already in the hospital. There was no regular new supply arriving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was Vukovar, in your view, cut off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In late September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it cut off by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like to move slightly to a different circumstance, and this is your personal living circumstance when the attacks started, which you mentioned was around the 24th of August. Now, on -- in August, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you travel there daily to the hospital from home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you travel? Did you drive? Did you walk? What was your means of reaching the hospital and back home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I needed some 20 minutes walking to the hospital, I mostly went on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did this take you to reach the hospital from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended from day to day. We always had to consider what was the good time to leave, because the shooting had already start in town. So sometimes we had to wait and sometimes we had to run, so it would take us only ten minutes. But on other days it could take up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you took your children out of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I took them from Vukovar in early September. I asked our director to allow me to leave. The conditions in town were such that we as medical personnel were indispensable. I asked the director for two days' leave so I could take the children out of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the medical director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why was it necessary to take your children out of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband and I decided that it was impossible for children to remain in town and be safe. I have to tell you that there was no basement in our house. Already at that time, there was several direct hits on our house and we had no place to take our children to. I went to work to the hospital every day, and we would take our children to the basement of our neighbour's house. Several days after that, after we started leaving our children in our neighbour's basement, that basement was hit as well. There was no safety for our children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time, were most other families living in their basements, if they were lucky enough to have one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why had they been forced to move into their basements? Because I assume these are residential properties where people are living.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Due to frequent shellings and hits on houses, private houses, where people lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you took your children to safety, your husband accompanied you. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Vukovar was clearly a dangerous place, so did your husband and yourself return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After we had taken our children away, we returned to the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time when your husband also left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He left in late September, and he didn't return anymore. I stayed in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't your husband return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because all communications had already been cut off. There was no longer any possibility to return to the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you clearly explained in your evidence, Vukovar was a dangerous place to be and your children had left and your husband had also left. So my question to you is: Why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a decision I had to make on my own after consulting my family. My job is a special kind of job. It's special in normal times, but it was especially important at moments like those. It was a very difficult decision to make. I had my family, my children, my husband. I also had my profession and the oath I had taken that I would responsibly do my job. You have to think very hard at such moments. You have to think about what you will gain and what you will lose. But if somebody had trusted me, believed me, that I was only going to take away my children, but if that person said, Please come back because we need you, what was I to do? And what prevailed was my job and my need to help people. I think my family understood me and supported me and helped me to make this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anyone in particular at the hospital ask you to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't say asked me. It was Dr. Bosanac personally who asked me, yes, to come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were your parents also living in Vukovar during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My parents stayed in our house and lived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how close to your house was your parents' house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We lived together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after your husband had left, did you still continue to visit your parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I visited my parents whenever it was possible. It was every few days until -- maybe I won't be quite precise, but until sometime in mid-October perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, with the Court's permission, I'd like to show the witness a map so that she can identify certain locations on it. So I would kindly ask the court officer if he could put on the screen so the witness could see the map with ERN 04626622. Now, Your Honours, just before this map comes up on everyone's screens, it is actually a map which the Prosecution has referred to before but it has not been exhibited. It's in the booklet of maps which the Chamber and, I believe, the Defence counsel were provided with. Now, with the permission of the Court, it's my intention that I ask that this map when it eventually appears - and it's the last one in the booklet - be exhibited in its blank format and then thereafter I would invite the witness to draw on the same map and then that can be given a fresh exhibit number. So in this way, we will always have the blank map as an exhibit to be called up for future reference. I believe the map is now on everyone's screens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see this map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is -- no, it hasn't come on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I wonder whether the court usher can be of assistance in perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: It's arrived. So does the Chamber and the Defence also have this map? It's clear for everyone?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is the map which I mentioned earlier which, with the Court's permission, I would like to have exhibited just in its blank format. It is an overview of the map of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And this will be exhibit number 59, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you could just find your bearings on that map. And I would invite the court usher to give you a pen and you will be able to draw on that map. And what I will invite you to do in a moment or two is to make some markings on the screen with that pen. So firstly, the hospital itself is already marked. Now, could you roughly mark whereabouts the area where your house was. Perhaps if you put a circle with an "A" there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could say that it was somewhere in the middle between the barracks and the hospital. The map is on a rather small scale, but it's around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I ask Your Honours that we could go into private session just for this part where these indications are made, the house. And also I will hopefully zoom in a little bit so that the witness can see more clearly for the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we finished dealing with the map, and I'd like now to take you back to the period after which your husband and children have now left Vukovar. Now, did there ever come a time after that when you shifted from your house to another place for overnight accommodation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In September, even before my husband left Vukovar, he spent a few days in the hospital with me. I definitely moved to the hospital, lived there, and worked there, and spent the whole day there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I slept together with the hospital staff in the ward, which was in the old part of the hospital. Later, together with all the others, in the basement of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you feel the need to move to the basement of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For safety, both the safety of the patients and the staff. Parts of the building were completely destroyed and could not be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did that mean that you couldn't stay on the second and first floors of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the fact that those parts of the hospital had already been shelled. On one such occasion, the shell hit part of our ward. I could no longer guarantee my patients' safety [Realtime transcript read in error "parents'"]. I couldn't leave them there physically because we couldn't be sure that the same part of the hospital would not be attacked again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as the battle progressed, was there an increase in the number of patients who was admitted into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After August, the number of patients increased considerably; it grew daily. There were days when there were between 50 and 80 patients a day. The number was sometimes so large, and I can't be precise about it, but it was over 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of patients were these? Were they fighters? Men? Women? Children? Civilian? What kind of people were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely all kinds. Children, civilians, women, men, anyone who was injured or sick, anyone who needed help, medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this include any wounded or injured JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. I think there were three members of the JNA who were treated in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small intervention in the transcript. Page 26, line 15, I heard the witness say she could no longer guarantee her patients' safety. The transcript says her parents' safety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these JNA wounded who were brought into the hospital, were they treated worse than any other patients or better than? How were they treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely the same as every patient and every human being who needed medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they kept separately from the other patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were in a separate room, the three of them together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that room guarded or was there any closed-offness to that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was under supervision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you think that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of the specific situation we were in. These were wartime conditions. The JNA was seen -- I apologise for the expression, but they were seen as an occupying force, as the other side, the opposing side. And it could happen that people who had been injured or people who had been wounded in any way had a negative attitude towards those people. But they were just simply people who had been wounded and who needed assistance, and we had to be absolutely professional. It was our job to provide assistance and also to protect them. If they were our patients, we had to guarantee their safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier you'd explained in your evidence that it wasn't possible to live on the first or second floors of the hospital because it had been shelled. Now, what kind of anti-aircraft or other weapons did you have in the hospital from which you were firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never heard that we had anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you're aware, then, the hospital wasn't firing at the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- as now I'd like to move to the part where we're drawing towards the end of the battle. And was there anyone in the hospital who was speaking to the JNA about the bombardment of the hospital or the conditions in the hospital? Did anyone complain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question a little bit. I may not have understood every part of it correctly. Do you mean what persons negotiated?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If we could start -- breakdown the question. I apologise, it was a bit lengthy. Who negotiated with the JNA regarding what was happening at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was Dr. Bosanac who negotiated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so far as you are aware, she was keeping the JNA informed of the conditions at the hospital and what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro was a surgeon, the chief of our surgery ward at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was also involved in treating the injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm coming again to the period where the battle is nearly over. When did you first learn that there would be an evacuation of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the last days that there was talk of that, on the 18th. I might pinpoint that as the day the town fell. And there began to be talk of evacuating the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, if you're now moving on to a distinct segment, that's probably a convenient time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There have been some redactions, so we must resume at 11.00. We'll adjourn for a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just before the break we were coming to the actual part of the evacuation at the hospital. Now, just before I come to that, do you know roughly how many people died in the hospital during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, some ten days before the fall of the town there were over 600 people who died in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these people buried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially, while it was still possible, the corpses were taken to the local cemeteries. However, in the last days, due to the intensity of the attacks, it was impossible to continue with that practice. According to my information, the bodies were taken to a spot near the hospital. I think that it was called the old port building where they placed the bodies of those who died and were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned just before the break that it was Dr. Bosanac who was involved in negotiations with the JNA. Now, slightly prior to the JNA coming to the hospital, did many townspeople come to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That lasted for several days or several evenings. It was around the 17th of November. Simply speaking, a large number of residents started spontaneously coming to the hospital. It's hard to estimate the number of people. It would be impossible to describe that scene. They spontaneously came to the hospital compound, entered the hospital. I would call it a state of chaos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I will be wrong if I say that there were about 1.000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were -- what kind of people were these? Were they former combatants, women? What sort of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were women, children, elderly. Had you seen them, you would have seen distorted faces of sorry-looking people, looking miserable. Everybody who remained in town came to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did they come to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The notion of a hospital before the war and after the war, it coincides with the notion of security, a place where one comes seeking refuge. That was the only place that remained in town, the hospital. And in the minds of all people, that represented a place where they could still seek salvation, protection, anything. That was what the hospital meant to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned on the 18th about Dr. Bosanac mentioning the evacuation. What were you actually told about the evacuation? How would it be carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that the evacuation would be carried out under the supervision of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who would be responsible for the patients' care during the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be absolutely us as their doctors and nurses. But in addition to that, the International Red Cross was supposed to supervise the entire process of evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did the JNA first arrive at the hospital in November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them for the first time on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much resistance was put up to the entry of the JNA into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None at all. There was no resistance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were in the hospital that time yourself. What was the prevailing atmosphere in the hospital when the JNA entered? What was the mood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's hard to convey sentiments. But all of us were afraid. We didn't know what was going to happen, how it was going to happen. We didn't know what was going on at all and where the Red Cross was, the Red Cross which was supposed to be there and to supervise the process. We didn't know who was in charge of us, of the entire hospital. It's very hard to describe these feelings to you, but I think that what dominated among everybody was the fear and insecurity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you explain why you personally felt this fear and insecurity if, as you mentioned earlier, that you believe the JNA had come to liberate you? Why would you be afraid of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The notion of liberation -- excuse me, but who were they supposed to liberate us from? We led a normal life. We didn't call upon anybody to come and liberate us. To liberate us from whom? From myself? From my friends? From my home? This notion of liberation is something that I understand differently. On the other hand, if somebody shoots at you for so many months, can you then perceive that as liberation or as something else? Certainly not liberation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what something else did you perceive it as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, I have to emphasise that I don't know how to define and I don't know what proper word to use to describe that. Once again, I apologise if I use an inappropriate term, but I consider that occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned you first saw the JNA enter the hospital on 19th November. What were the conditions like in the hospital then when they entered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions that you wouldn't believe people would be able to survive under, let alone work under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any comments made by any of the JNA regarding these working conditions that you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I happened to stand behind a group of soldiers who entered the hospital and who looked at the area. I think that the best description I can give you is the comment they uttered. Is it possible to live and work under these conditions? Is it possible that they really stayed here? I think no further comment is needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did you stay between the night of the 19th and the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in my office together with other staff members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would now like to turn to the morning of the 20th of November. So on the morning of the 20th November, did a particular staff member come and seek you out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning on the 20th of November at around 7.00 in the morning, Nurse Binazija came to my room, accompanied by a JNA member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what role did Nurse Binazija play in the hospital, and do you remember her second name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nurse Binazija Kolesar was the head nurse in the surgery ward at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when she came to you with this other person, what did she want you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When she came into my room, she had with her a list on a sheet of paper. She read out two names and she asked those two people to leave the room and stand outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I would just like to clarify this. You mention that Nurse Kolesar came to you with a JNA person. Now, did she take you anywhere first or did you remain in that same place when you had this discussion about the two names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We didn't go anywhere else. It was right there in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened after these two names were called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman who accompanied her asked me to describe the type of injuries that these persons had, what type of injuries those were, and he asked to look at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you explain to him the type of injuries they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of these two patients and what their injuries were, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This had to do with Mr. Holjevac and Mr. Bradaric. Shall I describe the injuries to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Holjevac had a fractured right arm above the elbow and a plaster on it. Mr. Bradaric had an injury of an eardrum, slight injury in his eye resulting from dust, and a cut on his arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many patients did you have under your care at that time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you asked about all 25 of these patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Just the two of them, the two names that I gave you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what were the names being called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a sheet of paper that Mrs. Binazija held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when these two patients were called out, where were they told to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were told to get ready and to leave the room. They were told to go to another part of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this brief meeting between the nurse, your patients, and the JNA member, where did you then go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nurse Binazija told us that all medical staff was supposed to assemble in the premise of the surgical clinic or the plaster room. At any rate, in a certain area that belonged to the surgical ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of us went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who chaired this meeting, if you like? Who was in charge of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person who chaired the meeting was Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know it was Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin introduced himself upon meeting us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, what did he tell the assembled meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting lasted perhaps half an hour or 45 minutes, around that time. And during that time, he spoke to us in general about the political situation, about the breakup of Yugoslavia, how that came about. He told us that he understood us as medical staff, he realised that we just did our job and that it was natural that we did so, and that he wouldn't take that against us. It was along those lines. I cannot convey verbatim his words, but the discussion mostly focussed on that. I have to admit that I didn't follow closely his words throughout that time because my thoughts were simply not organised, and I didn't fully follow everything that the gentleman said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who, in your view, after this meeting was in charge of the hospital? Was it still Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At the meeting we were told that Dr. Bosanac was no longer our director and that they had taken over the hospital and were in charge, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it who said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mention that this meeting was going on for about 45 minutes. Now, whilst this meeting was in progress with Mr. Sljivancanin, did you notice anything unusual happening in the corridor outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time, as I was standing towards the back of the room near the door which was opened and which faced the corridor of the reception area of the surgical ward, I turned around and left the room. And at that moment I saw a group of my patients who were being led away by the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many medical staff were accompanying your patients with the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not a single member of medical staff accompanying them. All of us were in that meeting at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many members of the Red Cross or other monitors did you see accompanying your patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you think these patients were being led away by the JNA in an ordinary fashion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all happened so quickly that it didn't seem to us like a normal course of an evacuation as we believe it should take place. It simply happened too quickly, as if something was being concealed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while this removal of the patients was taking place, you say, where were most of the hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them were in the meeting with Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what were you able to conclude about the timing and the manner in which these patients were being removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time it was difficult for me to comprehend why this was unfolding in this way or where these people were being taken and why we were not present there, we as those who cared for them until that time. We simply didn't know where they were going. Nobody told us anything about that. But we were still hoping that everything would be all right, that everything should be all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to be very clear about this. Most of these people who were being led away by the JNA while the hospital staff was in the meeting, what were they? Were they civilians? Were they patients? What largely was their make-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who were led away were precisely the patients of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many firearms did they each have on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can guarantee you that not a single of my patient had a single piece of weaponry on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did some of these patients also have medical appendages on them or other means to assist them in their recovery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this line of questioning of my learned friend is a typical example of leading questioning. Because on page 37, line 16, there was a question that was leading in a way but could be acceptable. And the Prosecutor asked the witness for her impression, and she answered in very specific terms; namely, that at the time it was very difficult to comprehend what was happening. She gave her own conclusion. Following that, all of the questions that were put after that were such that they called for a contradicting answer from the witness, and I think that it is inappropriate because the witness has already given us her conclusion at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Many of the questions, Mr. Lukic, are seeking more precise detail about specific issues. So in that respect, I can't agree with you. But I can certainly agree that the last couple of witnesses -- questions and some earlier ones were leading in form. So, Mr. Agha, if you could be more careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now, with the Court's permission I'd like to show the witness a sketch plan, and this is a sketch plan of a part of the hospital drawn by the witness or at least produced under her guidance. And it's ter number is 226. So if I could kindly ask the court officer to put that on the screen, that would be very helpful. And for further precision, the ERN is 00596037, if that helps. So does the Chamber as well as the witness and the learned Defence counsel have this on their screen, this plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, was this sketch together with markings, numbers connotating to words, positions, was this drawn up under your guidance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what actually is it a sketch plan of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the basement area of the hospital where we stayed during the war together with our patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on this sketch plan on the lower part, there are numbers correlating to words. For example, number 1 is by a corridor. Now, are all these correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can see they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I kindly ask you, with the assistance of the court usher, because I'd like you to do a little drawing on this sketch, to make a marking for me, please. I apologise for the delays, Witness. Now, you can see the sketch of the hospital. Now, which number room was it that Mr. Sljivancanin held his meeting? Can you please circle it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please indicate with the marker where you were standing, perhaps if you could put an "A" where you saw these patients being led out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could kindly just draw with an arrow and perhaps mark it with a "B" the direction in which the patients you saw were coming from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you then show the direction in which they were being taken to, please, by the marker and mark that "C."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's towards the exit, here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, may I ask that this sketch be saved with the markings on and be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all with this particular sketch.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 61, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the meeting with Mr. Sljivancanin, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the room where I stayed; that is, my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From there we returned to another meeting, which was held together with Mr. Ivankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic was a surgeon in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of his relatives also come to the hospital between the 18th and 20th of November, so far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what I heard, his son came together with the members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his son a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a member of a paramilitary unit, but I cannot assert that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, coming back to the meeting with Dr. Ivankovic, what was told to you at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that meeting we were told that as doctors we could decide whether to remain at the hospital, whether to go to Serbia or to Croatia. Each one of us could make a decision about his or her future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long, roughly, was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted ten or 15 minutes, not longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that meeting I went back to my office, that is the place where I had been living, to collect my things. And then I went out to the place where those of us who had decided to go to Croatia were supposed to gather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that meeting with Dr. Ivankovic, what other interactions did you have with your patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I no longer had any contacts with my patients, in view of the fact that the hospital was already empty. It had been emptied of all my patients I found, or rather saw. Only Mrs. Zahora who was also a patient of mine, a lady.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you went to check on your patients, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Empty beds and empty rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you made a list of your patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Several evenings before the evacuation was planned, I made a list of the patients I had been taking care of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you to make that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told -- the request came from Dr. Bosanac. She said we should each make a list of our patients. She didn't tell that to us personally, but that's what was conveyed to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of making this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In such situations, it's professional for every staff member to care for the people they had been taking care of up to that point. We envisioned a transport of patients, and each doctor was supposed to be close to the patients they were looking after in order to be able to assist them during the transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, with the permission of the Court, I'd like to put up an exhibit which actually -- a proposed exhibit, which actually is that list. And for the benefit of the court clerk, it has a 65 ter number of 227 and ERN 00381949.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have the list on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a copy of the list which you made before your patients were removed from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many patients are listed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who actually is number 25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The technician, a member of the medical staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he wasn't actually a patient. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It says next to his name that he is a medical technician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the other 24 were patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did all of these patients on this list have genuine injuries which you were treating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you kindly identify the numbers of the -- those on your list who did not have genuine injury.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you can show me the next page of the list. I'm sorry, could you go back. Yes, now you can go on. Can you go on? Further. Number 16. For 17 I have a special explanation to give. Can we go further? 19. 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, referring to the names, or at least the numbers you have picked out, number 16, 19, and 20 who were not injured, can you explain why they were put on your list of patients.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it's difficult to explain. I'll ask you to try and understand. To explain this to someone who is listening now is very difficult. I apologise. The feelings are coming back to me of a time I don't like to speak about, but I will try to convey to you what I felt then and how we felt at the time and why I did this because it was purely my own decision. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you just --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you just pause a moment and collect yourself. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind that we are looking at this list and we are in public session, I only wanted to express my fears for the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Could we perhaps go into private session for -- just while we deal with the list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Private.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you discovered that most of your patients had gone, where did you then go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to collect my things, and then I left through the same exit. I went to the emergency ward, which is in the area in front of the new building. We awaited evacuation there, or rather, we awaited our departure towards Zagreb there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you then indeed evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that area we waited for some two hours. I left with a group of staff members, and we went to stand in front of the former court building where the buses waited for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were waiting to get on the buses, how many soldiers did you see and of what kind, could you distinguish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there were many soldiers in the hospital yard; they had arrived. That was the first time I saw people who did not have clear JNA insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of insignia did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had insignia with four letters S. They also had white feathers on their sleeves. Those were not regular army insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how would you describe these troops as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They looked terrifying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as well as these kind of troops, could you also distinguish whether there were regular JNA soldiers also there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were regular soldiers there who were moving in that area, entering the hospital, or just standing in that open area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were able to distinguish between the two kinds of soldiers, the regular JNA and the other, as you have called them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were evacuated, how many patients roughly came with you in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on my information, about 54.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your view, how many patients should there have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 300 and 400, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the whereabouts of these missing patients? Did they catch you up later en route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At the time we didn't know anything about their fate. We were hoping that they took perhaps another road and followed us, but at that time we knew nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge have most of them been found alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in general?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Out of those 300, unfortunately most of them are not alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wonder whether I should begin with cross-examination or are we perhaps ready for a break? That's why I'm looking upon you for guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was assessing that at the moment you rose. We think alike, Mr. Vasic, yes. I think it would be perhaps a good time at the moment to have a break and that enable the witness to rest for a little while before we continue. We will resume at a quarter to 1.00, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic will now have some questions for you. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Madam, let me introduce myself. I am Miroslav Vasic, attorney-at-law, defence counsel for Mr. Mrksic. In view of the fact that both of us speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to make a pause before answering my questions, so that the interpreters are given a chance to interpret that and so that I can turn off my microphone and thus protect your voice. Today you told us that Vukovar was a multi-ethnic town, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also said that in 1991 the relations that were up until that time harmonious started deteriorating and becoming less harmonious. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the relations start deteriorating even before the events in Borovo Selo that you described today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that the deterioration was more pronounced following that, but that is just my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were first multi-party elections held in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At that time, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the elections at the republic level in Croatia it was the Croatian Democratic Community that won?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Croatian Democratic Union, was it a party of persons who had nationalistic orientations and views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just like back then, I am not engaged in politics nowadays either. I never followed political developments so closely as to be able to say that that party was a party of Croats who held nationalistic views.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Vukovar in the local elections, the party that won was the SDP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Following that, Slavko Dokmanovic, who was a Serb, was elected president of the Municipal Assembly in Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether before May 1991, before the events you described in Borovo Selo, the National Guards Corps had already been founded in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the events of the 2nd of May in Borovo Selo. Can you tell us why the police, or rather, the MUP of Croatian members went to intervene in Borovo Selo? Do you know what caused it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only convey to you what I learned from reading papers at the time. This intervention was a result of some kind of an unrest, a riot, in Borovo Selo. But whether that is a correct interpretation or not, I really wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that there was some residents who rebelled there. Can you tell us what they rebelled against, what was the reason for their rebellion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would be better placed to answer your question, those who rebelled. I'm unable to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given that the first multi-party elections were held in 1991 in the territory of the entire former SFRY, I assume that you, as a citizen, followed the political and social developments in the country. Do you know that after these elections the constitution of Croatia was amended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know to what extent and I don't know precisely which portions of the constitution were amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these constitutional amendments also changed the status of the Serbian people, who until that time were a constituent nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that following the events in Borovo Selo, Slavko Dokmanovic, as president of the Municipal Assembly, publicly called upon all residents of Vukovar to decrease tension and find a peaceful resolution to all of the problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent that one was able to hear that on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Shortly thereafter, did Slavko Dokmanovic cease to perform duties as municipal president and was a government commissioner appointed by the Croatian government for Vukovar, a person who was a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Which period of time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to end of June, early July 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that a commissioner was appointed, a commissioner for Vukovar. Whether it was precisely then, during that period of time, if you say so, then most likely it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The commissioner, was he a member of the HDZ, despite the fact that it was the SDP that had won the elections in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to reiterate that neither then nor now am I interested in any political developments or political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. You were not interested in politics. Do you know that as early as May there were groups organised in the streets of Vukovar comprising members of Croatian ethnicity to defend Vukovar? Did you see something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that as early as the 4th of May, 1991 the name of the Vukovar radio station was changed and its director replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: From that day on, was the radio station called Croatian Radio Vukovar and was its Serb director replaced by a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was called Croatian Radio Vukovar. As for whether a Croat replaced a Serb, I have to tell you that I do not divide people upon that basis, upon them being Croats or Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Neither do I, Madam. However, I am describing the situation that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the economic sector of Vukovar a director was also replaced -- directors were also replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Directors were frequently replaced, and I don't think that I could say that it existed only during that period of time. This is something that frequently happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the institution where you worked, pursuant to the order issued by the Croatian government, the previous director was replaced by a new one. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether that was done pursuant to the government order, I wouldn't be able to say, but the director was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And instead of the former director, who was a Serb, a new director came, a Croat. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that Dr. Bosanac replaced Dr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I wasn't going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to mention any names in view of the protection measures, but all of us know what this pertains to. You told us that in the institution where you worked, the employees were of mixed national backgrounds. Following the events in Borovo Selo, did the Serbs employed in your institution start leaving and in large numbers, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that, yes, there were Serbs who were leaving, but also Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: From the people who were leaving and who were Serbs, did you hear that they did so because they feared for their own safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Be so kind and tell us what was the reason for the departure of physicians who were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that everybody has a right to assess whether they feel good in a certain place or not, whether they want to leave their jobs or the area where they live. However, we didn't discuss whether they were leaving because of their personal safety. It was up to each individual to determine whether they felt safe or not. In direct contacts, we did not have such exchanges, such conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there a decrease in the number of Serb patients coming to your institution during that same period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, the patients kept coming and we never asked anybody what their nationality was when admitting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, following the events in Borovo Selo were the wounded MUP patients admitted to the institution where you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean? Admitted as patients or housed in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I said was whether the wounded members of the MUP were admitted as patients.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naturally. Everybody who was injured was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: These wounded MUP members, were they also guarded by the police during their stay in the hospital, armed police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer your question because I didn't work in that ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You must know that after the 2nd of May a Crisis Staff was established in the hospital pursuant to the order of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will get to that topic later on as well. But tell me, was it the task of the Crisis Staff to put the hospital on alert and ensure that it was prepared to admit the wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the specific tasks and job descriptions, I wouldn't be able to tell you that because I was not a member of the Crisis Staff.
