However, the hospital functioned under different conditions. And I think that that was their task to adjust the function of the hospital to the newly created circumstances. However, I myself was not a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you guessed correctly; that was precisely the question that I was about to put to you. Now, please tell me whether during that period of time preparations were conducted to use the atomic shelter that existed within your institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to the month of May, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to something that I asked you earlier and that has to do with the wounded MUP members treated in the hospital. Did their presence in the hospital lead to the reduction in the number of Serb patients coming to the hospital at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in my ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Following the events in Borovo Selo, for a while there was no escalation of the conflict. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In early June 1991, were the roadblocks set up in the area leaving Borovo Selo and entering Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was unable to see that, therefore I can neither confirm nor deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know the person called Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. For the transcript let me repeat. Mr. Tomislav Mercep. Do you know what his duty was in Vukovar municipality in May and June 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure I'll be able to give you the title correctly, but I think he was in charge of the defence of the town. I apologise if the description is not correct because I'm not absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear that in March 1991, that is before the conflict in Borovo Selo, Mr. Tomislav Mercep reviewed the ZNG in Bogdanovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when did you first hear of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear about the ZNG, but as for the time period I really couldn't pinpoint the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you hear under the auspices of what political party the ZNG was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that throughout June in Vukovar, where you lived, explosives were set in houses owned by Serbs that the kiosks of the newspaper Borba were blown up, a Serb newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that there were rumours going around that in this period some citizens of Serb ethnicity went missing in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were rumours going around about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you lived in Vukovar for a long time, you must know where the barracks is, the JNA barracks, where it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also know that this barracks in Vukovar was there long before any tensions or conflicts arose, several dozen years before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that in the summer of 1991 at one point the barracks was surrounded and blocked by members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that at one point the barracks was attacked by members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Vukovar is a relatively small town and that something like the blocking of a barracks and attacks on a barrack does not happen every day, I have to ask you whether people talked about this in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time various stories went around, but what you don't see you don't believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us today that the attack on Vukovar began on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there had to be a reason for the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There really should be a big reason to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you didn't hear about the blockade of the barracks and the exclusion of water and electricity from the barracks, on the 24th of August, 1991 were two JNA planes shot down while flying over the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to mention that I was not in town those -- in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about this event on your return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could hear that in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On your return to town, did you come across ZNG defence lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the military sense? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you come across checkpoints held by members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area where I lived, in the centre where I moved around, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the entrance into Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 25th I went in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So when after the 24th of August you were on your way back into Vukovar, did you run across any checkpoints held by members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the people manning those checkpoints were armed, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On your return to Vukovar, were you aware who was the commander of the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, quite truthfully, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us go back now to the atomic shelter that has already been mentioned. Tell me, how many beds were in this atomic shelter when it was prepared to receive the wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you the precise number at this moment. I can only recall and count the number of beds I remember, but I may be wrong about the number. Initially, I think ten or 15, but please don't hold me to this; it may not be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, over a prolonged period of time were patients from your hospital evacuated to Vinkovci on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one period when it was still possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you aware that throughout the time of these events from August to November 1991, a helicopter landed on the stadium near the hospital which arrived from Croatia bringing in medicines, food, and other necessities for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in October, more precisely on the 18th of October, 1991, a convoy was organised under the auspices of the Medecins Sans Frontieres and that they evacuated 112 wounded from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Today you mentioned certain wounded JNA soldiers. I would like to ask you whether you knew Ivan Zivkovic, a wounded JNA soldier admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have access to the wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you have no knowledge of his evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who had access to the wounded soldiers and who might know about the questions I was about to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the type of injuries they had. It was the doctors that these patients needed. At the time, they did not need my specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If the injuries were caused by projectiles or shrapnel, we should ask the doctors in the surgical ward. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Dr. Njavro. You said that he was the chief surgeon. Do you know when he was appointed chief surgeon and by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be certain about the precise time, but I think it was when the Crisis Staff was created. I cannot say with certainty what date it was really.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us in connection with those three soldiers that you knew they were in hospital and that they were in a separate room. Did you know that they were guarded by Damir Samardzic in a room under orders from Ivica Arbanas, who was the commander of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was an order issued by the ZNG that surgical interventions on wounded members of the ZNG could be conducted only by Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I can agree with this. I may be wrong, but I know that all colleagues participated in the work and that no attention was paid to anything like that. It was according to need. But perhaps you should ask other surgeons about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When speaking of wounded patients in the hospital, can you tell me how the list of wounded was made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in general? The admittance of all patients to the hospital? Did you mean that? Could you please be more precise in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period from August to November 1991, how the wounded and other patients went to the hospital were listed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially while each ward was working individually, each ward had its own documentation. When we became a single hospital, a single ward, then there was one entrance and the admittance was organised so that there was only one admittance to hospital. But it could happen for a patient to come to you personally bypassing the reception desk. I think that's a proper description.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then the register book would be updated if a patient bypassed the reception desk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume that this information was entered into the register book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think they were all entered. There were omissions from time to time, and we would intervene. It might happen for an omission to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But there were register books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. There had to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: To facilitate information about the condition of the patients, apart from this register book, did you keep any kind of notebooks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every patient had to have a temperature chart, just as in the protocol of every hospital, with the patient's name and their medical history. It's the standard documentation a patient has to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as for the anaesthesia register books, you said that initially each ward had its own register book. Now, did the -- did there exist a register book for all of those patients who were given anaesthesia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to the documents we mentioned, were there perhaps notebooks where they entered by hand a patient's name, wound, address, the date of admittance, status, and so on, in order to provide information to those who came inquiring about the patients? Do you know perhaps who kept such notebooks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was nothing of the sort in my ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the hospital itself, at the level of the hospital, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There -- every patient must be registered and have its own document -- have his own documentation. As for these separate notebooks, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because Witness Binazija Kolesar told us that such notebooks were kept and that this information was entered. That's why I asked you about that. Did you hear this from her and did these notebooks exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If she says so, then that's how it was. She was the head nurse in the surgical ward and she took care of a lot of things, including administrative matters. If this is what she said, then it must be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether in addition to these register books, temperature charts, medical histories, and notebooks any other records of patients existed in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on my information, we had to record patients in a daily -- in a central document where patients were daily recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You are probably referring to the central register book where all the patients who enter the hospital are recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how it should be. That's what the rule is, but as I've already mentioned there were some problems with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the hospital, or rather, the hospital Crisis Staff had electronic communication with the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, or Ministry of Health of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there were telephone contacts, but with whom exactly I really couldn't say, as I was not a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a radio link between the hospital and the ZNG unit commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can give the same answer I gave to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you told us that from the 17th of November there were no combat activities in Vukovar, that they ceased.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened between the 17th and the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then the citizens of Vukovar started streaming towards the hospital; that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: They came to the hospital because at that time the hospital was a safe place, as the artillery fire had ceased, the bombing and everything else that affected the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to civilians, a large number of ZNG and MUP members also came to the hospital for the same reasons, expecting to find safety there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that you personally didn't see them, but did you hear of their arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When do you think you heard about them arriving in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my previous examination I never mentioned something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Madam, did you give a statement to the investigators of the Prosecution on the 14th and 22nd of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You signed the statement, and following that you came to testify in a trial here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that time, when you came to testify here you were shown your 1995 statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You just had to tell me which statement exactly you had in mind. That's what you should have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I had in mind the statement you gave in June of 1995 where you stated that as the fall of the remaining part of the town was inevitable at the time, the soldiers dropped their weapons and put on civilian clothes. Many of them put on plasters and bandages to pass themselves off as the wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But there was -- there was several additional words there that indicated that this is something that I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you are referring to this additional clarification, you are referring to the clarification given in October of this year. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Some time ago I asked you about when you heard that the members of ZNG and MUP arrived in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise if I did not understand your question. But this is something that I heard once we arrived in Zagreb and once all of us started discussing the events in Vukovar. We did that upon our arrival in Zagreb. I hope this clarifies the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that some people from the hospital were aware of the arrival of the ZNG and MUP members? You talked about this, so somebody must have known about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't explain that. I can't tell you whether somebody from the hospital knew about that. I'm just telling you what we discussed later on. There were many of us, a thousand people at least, and we discussed about what had happened to each of us individually. Now, who specifically mentioned this, I wouldn't be able to tell you that. There were just stories going around. As for whether somebody from the hospital knew about this, I really wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If those were just stories, stories shared by a large number of people, can you explain us, then, why did you believe it necessary to mention this to the Prosecutor in 1995 and why was this included in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was then asked by them, just as I'm now asked by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you will agree that in your 1995 statement you never mentioned about just hearing this. Was that how you described it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I stated it precisely in those terms, even back then. This is why I'm very careful today because I want to ensure that I understand everything correctly, and I ask for clarifications in order to be able to give accurate answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Upon giving your statement to the Prosecutor, was the statement read out to you in Croatian and did you affirm that you understood the statement and that you accepted it as your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been a long time, and whether the statement was read out to me, it probably should have been; most likely it was. But I also must mention that it is possible that I overlooked certain things or failed to mention them. This is why I'm being extra careful today in seeking clarification. When you describe emotionally traumatic events that affected you deeply, then you will certainly agree with me that it is possible to overlook a word here and there that might be important but that, due to your excitement, you are simply unable to recollect right then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you are able to confirm that you did sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if this is the proper time for adjournment. Should I cease bothering the witness with additional questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know that "bothering" is the right word, Mr. Vasic, but we certainly have reached the time when we must adjourn for the day, and I was waiting for you to appear to reach a point where I wouldn't disturb a line of questions. So we will break now. I must ask you if you would return tomorrow to continue your evidence. We must adjourn now for the day. We continue the hearing tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
